$comment: Employment policy set — generated when the company plans to hire within 12 months. The California-conditioned clauses are the spec's own §2.1 example (meal break, rest period, PTO accrual).

clauses.title: At-Will Employment
clauses.rationale: At-will status is the default everywhere in this library except by contract, but it is eroded by handbook language promising process. Saying it plainly, and limiting who can change it, is the protection.
clauses.body: Employment with the Company is [[at-will employment|at-will employment]] and may be terminated by either party at any time, with or without cause or notice. No manager, and no statement in any handbook or policy, alters this status except in a writing signed by the {{principalTitle}}.

clauses.title: Classification
clauses.rationale: Misclassification is the most common and most expensive wage-and-hour error, and it is decided by duties and salary rather than by job title.
clauses.body: Each employee shall be classified as [[exempt employee|exempt employee]] or non-exempt based on their actual duties and compensation, not on job title. Classification shall be documented at hire and reviewed whenever duties change materially. Non-exempt employees shall record all hours worked.

clauses.title: Work Authorization
clauses.rationale: Form I-9 must be completed within three business days of the first day of work. The penalty attaches to the paperwork failure itself, independent of anyone's actual status.
clauses.body: The Company shall complete Form I-9 for every employee within three (3) business days of their first day of work, retain the forms separately from personnel files, and apply the same documentary requirements to all employees without regard to national origin or citizenship status.

clauses.title: Written Offer Requirements
clauses.rationale: Several states require a written wage notice at hire. A standard offer template satisfies that and prevents inconsistent side promises.
clauses.body: Every offer shall be made in writing and shall state the position, the rate and basis of pay, the pay schedule, the classification determined under <<xr:emp_classification>>, and any conditions of employment. Verbal assurances about job security or future compensation are not authorized.

clauses.title: Independent Contractor Classification
clauses.benchmark: Present in 58% of employment policy sets
clauses.rationale: California's ABC test in particular makes most contractors employees. The exposure is back wages, taxes, and penalties across the whole engagement.
clauses.body: Before engaging any individual as an independent contractor, the Company shall evaluate the engagement under the test applicable in {{opStateLong}} and document the analysis. Contractors shall not be given Company email, fixed schedules, or supervision of employees, and shall sign an agreement assigning intellectual property to the Company.

clauses.title: Overtime
clauses.rationale: Federal overtime is weekly; several states add a daily threshold. Paying on the federal rule alone underpays in those states.
clauses.body: Non-exempt employees shall receive overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked over forty (40) in a workweek, and at any additional rate required by the law of {{opStateLong}}. Overtime must be paid whether or not it was authorized in advance.

clauses.title: Meal Period Policy
clauses.rationale: California meal period violations carry a one-hour premium per day and are among the most frequently litigated wage claims.
clauses.body: A non-exempt employee may not be employed for a work period of more than five (5) hours per day without being provided a meal period of not less than thirty (30) minutes, nor for more than ten (10) hours per day without a second period of not less than thirty (30) minutes. Because the duty attaches to a work period of more than five hours, the first period has to be provided before the fifth hour is complete. The first period may be waived by mutual consent of the Company and the employee where the total work period for the day is no more than six (6) hours; the second may be waived by mutual consent where the total hours worked is no more than twelve (12) hours and the first was not waived. The Company's duty is to relieve the employee of all duty for the period and relinquish control over how the time is spent; it is not a duty to ensure that no work is done, so a compliant period the employee chooses to work through owes nothing. A period during which the employee is not relieved of all duty is an on-duty meal period, counted as time worked, and is permitted only where the nature of the work prevents relief from all duty and the parties have signed a written agreement stating that the employee may revoke it in writing at any time. Where a compliant meal period is not provided, one (1) additional hour of pay is owed for that workday at the employee's regular rate of compensation — which means the same thing as the regular rate of pay used for overtime, and so takes in non-discretionary payments and not the base hourly rate alone. Meal periods must be recorded and those punches may not be rounded; records showing a missed, short or delayed period raise a rebuttable presumption of a violation, which the Company can meet with evidence that a compliant period was provided or the premium paid. Section 512 does not reach employees in certain occupations covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, or the motion picture and broadcasting agreements described in the section.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §512 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 95 (SB 693), eff. Jan. 1, 2026)
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §226.7 (both enacted versions; the version operative Jan. 1, 2027 was read alongside the current one)
Department of Industrial Relations — IWC Order No. 4-2001, §11 (Meal Periods), effective January 1, 2002 as amended
CourtListener — Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004
CourtListener — Ferra v. Loews Hollywood Hotel, LLC (2021) 11 Cal.5th 858
CourtListener — Donohue v. AMN Services, LLC (2021) 11 Cal.5th 58

defects: Wage Order No. 4-2001 was read for the meal-period provision because it is the order that covers professional, technical, clerical and mechanical occupations. The clause is inserted for every California employer regardless of industry, and the other sixteen orders were not read. An employer under Order 5, 7, 11, 12 or 16 may owe something different, and this clause does not say so.
The clause states the premium as owed "for that workday" without resolving whether a meal violation and a rest violation on the same day are separately payable. That question was not researched here.

Whether a meal-period waiver has to be in writing was not resolved. Section 512(a) and Wage Order 4 §11(A) both say "mutual consent" and neither requires a writing; the written-agreement requirement in the section applies to on-duty meal periods. The clause follows the text, but a reader may take the silence as permission to rely on an oral waiver, which no source read here endorses.

clauses.title: Rest Period Policy
clauses.rationale: Rest periods are paid time and cannot be combined with meal periods or used to leave early. The premium is the same one hour per day.
clauses.body: The Company authorizes and permits non-exempt employees to take rest periods, which insofar as practicable shall be in the middle of each work period. Rest time is based on total hours worked daily at the rate of ten (10) minutes net rest time per four (4) hours or major fraction thereof: ten minutes for a shift of three and one-half to six hours, twenty minutes for more than six and up to ten hours, thirty minutes for more than ten and up to fourteen, and so on. No rest period need be authorized where the employee's total daily work time is less than three and one-half (3½) hours. Rest periods are counted as hours worked and there is no deduction from wages for them. A rest period must be off duty: the Company must relieve the employee of all duties and relinquish control over how the time is spent, and may not require the employee to remain on call. Where a rest period is not provided, one (1) additional hour of pay is owed for that workday at the employee's regular rate of compensation, which takes in non-discretionary payments and not the base hourly rate alone. Rest periods are scheduled so that they are not combined with a meal period or taken in exchange for leaving early — NOT VERIFIED: no provision of Wage Order No. 4-2001 or the Labor Code read for this rebuild states that rule, and it is carried here as Company practice following from the "middle of each work period" requirement, not as a legal requirement. The Legislature has displaced the off-duty rule for a registered security officer employed by a registered private patrol operator under a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, who may be required to remain on the premises and on call; that exception reaches no other occupation.

California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §226.7, including subdivision (f) (security officers)
CourtListener — Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court (2012) 53 Cal.4th 1004
CourtListener — Augustus v. ABM Security Services, Inc. (2016) 2 Cal.5th 257
CourtListener — Ferra v. Loews Hollywood Hotel, LLC (2021) 11 Cal.5th 858

defects: The previous citation named "IWC Wage Order (industry-specific)" — a body of law with no provision inside it, so nothing could be looked up. It has been replaced with Order No. 4-2001 §12, which is the order covering professional, technical, clerical and mechanical occupations. That is a real provision but it is not necessarily the reader's order: the clause is inserted for every California employer and the other sixteen orders were not read.

The sentence about not combining rest with meal periods, and not trading a rest period for an early departure, is carried with an explicit NOT VERIFIED marker. It is standard practice and it follows from the "middle of each work period" language, but no primary text read for this rebuild imposes it.
Whether the ten-minute period runs from when the employee reaches the break area, and whether the employer must relieve the employee for the walking time, was not researched and is not addressed.

clauses.title: PTO Accrual
clauses.rationale: Accrued vacation is wages in California. A use-it-or-lose-it policy is unenforceable and creates a wage claim at every departure.
clauses.body: Accrued and unused vacation is wages under California law and is paid out at termination at the final rate of pay. The Company does not operate a use-it-or-lose-it policy; accrual may be capped at a reasonable multiple of the annual accrual rate but may not be forfeited.

clauses.title: Final Pay Timing
clauses.rationale: California waiting time penalties accrue at a full day of wages per day late, up to thirty days, for a payroll timing error alone.
clauses.body: An employee who is discharged must be paid all wages earned and unpaid immediately at the time of discharge. An employee who quits must be paid within seventy-two (72) hours, or at the time of quitting if they gave seventy-two hours' previous notice; an employee who quits without that notice may request payment by mail, and the date of mailing is then the date of payment. Final pay includes accrued vested vacation under <<xr:emp_pto>> and any meal or rest period premium owed, which is a wage for this purpose and not merely a penalty. Several groups are on their own clocks and are not covered by the general rule: a seasonal layoff in the curing, canning or drying of perishable fruit, fish or vegetables is payable within a reasonable time not exceeding seventy-two (72) hours; an oil drilling layoff within twenty-four (24) hours excluding Saturdays, Sundays and holidays; and temporary services, motion picture, print shoot and live theatrical or concert venue employees are governed by Labor Code sections 201.3, 201.5, 201.6 and 201.9. A wilful failure to pay makes the employee's wages continue as a penalty at the same daily rate until paid or until an action is commenced, and for no more than thirty (30) days. The penalty does not follow automatically from lateness: an employer that reasonably and in good faith disputes that the wages are due has not acted wilfully, and an employee who hides, avoids payment, or refuses a full tender takes no benefit for that time.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §§200–209, read as a whole (§§201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.7, 201.9, 202, 203)
CourtListener — Naranjo v. Spectrum Security Services, Inc. (2024) 17 Cal.5th 1 (good faith dispute defeats "wilful")
CourtListener — Naranjo v. Spectrum Security Services, Inc. (2022) 13 Cal.5th 93 (premium pay is wages for §§201–203)

defects: The good-faith-dispute rule is stated in the clause on the authority of Naranjo (2024), which describes it as "long established law" and cites In re Trombley, Barnhill and 8 C.C.R. §13520. The regulation that actually defines a good faith dispute could not be read: the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy. The clause therefore states that a good faith dispute defeats wilfulness without stating what makes a dispute good faith.

Labor Code §201 also carries a state-employer deferral scheme in subdivisions (b) to (d) that was read and deliberately not carried, on the ground that no user of this corpus is the State of California. If that assumption is wrong the clause is incomplete for such an employer.

The sections listed for the industry exceptions were identified from §203(a)'s own cross-references and from §201.7; §§201.3, 201.5, 201.6 and 201.9 were seen in the article listing but their operative deadlines were not read in full, so the clause names them rather than stating their rules.

clauses.title: Itemized Wage Statements
clauses.rationale: Wage statement claims are commonly added to any other wage claim because the defect is visible on the face of the document.
clauses.body: Every wage payment shall be accompanied by an itemized statement showing gross wages, total hours worked for non-exempt employees, all deductions, net wages, the pay period dates, the employee’s name and last four digits of their identification number, and the Company’s legal name and address as stated in <<xr:charter_name>>.

clauses.title: Paid Sick Leave
clauses.rationale: Paid sick leave is mandatory in both states at low employee counts, and the accrual and carryover mechanics differ from vacation.
clauses.body: Employees accrue paid sick leave as required by the law of {{opStateLong}}, beginning on the first day of employment and available for use as provided by that law. Sick leave is tracked separately from vacation, and unused sick leave carries over subject to any statutory cap.

clauses.title: Employee Invention Assignment
clauses.rationale: Founder IP assignment does not cover employees. Every hire needs their own assignment signed before the first day of work.
clauses.body: Every employee shall sign an invention assignment and confidentiality agreement before their first day of work, assigning to the Company all inventions and works created in the scope of employment, and including any statutory carve-out required in {{opStateLong}}. An assignment signed after work has begun may require separate consideration to be enforceable.

clauses.title: Non-Compete Prohibition Notice
clauses.rationale: Since AB 1076 it is unlawful to include or attempt to enforce a non-compete in California, and notice to affected current and former employees was required.
clauses.body: The Company shall not require any employee working in California to sign a non-compete or customer non-solicitation covenant. Such provisions are void under California law regardless of where the agreement was signed or which state’s law it names. The Company protects its interests through the confidentiality and invention assignment obligations in <<xr:emp_ip>> instead.

clauses.title: Anti-Harassment Policy and Training
clauses.rationale: A published policy with a real reporting path is the first element of the employer's defense, and training is mandatory at low headcount in several states.
clauses.body: The Company shall maintain a written anti-harassment and anti-retaliation policy with at least two reporting channels, at least one of which does not run through the employee’s direct manager. The Company shall provide the training required by {{opStateLong}} at the intervals and headcount thresholds that law specifies.

clauses.title: Confidentiality
clauses.benchmark: Present in 88% of employee policy sets
clauses.rationale: A confidentiality obligation without the whistleblower carve-out can itself be unlawful, so the two belong in the same clause.
clauses.body: Employees shall not use or disclose Company confidential information during or after employment, except as required by law. Nothing in this policy prohibits an employee from reporting a suspected violation of law to a government agency, participating in an agency investigation, or discussing wages and working conditions with coworkers.

clauses.title: Arbitration of Employment Disputes
clauses.benchmark: Present in 41% of employment policy sets
clauses.rationale: Genuinely two-sided. Arbitration limits class exposure but is unenforceable for some claims, cannot be a condition of employment in some states, and shifts the fee burden to the employer.
clauses.body: If the Company adopts arbitration, the agreement shall be a separate signed document rather than a handbook provision, shall be mutual, shall require the Company to bear arbitration costs beyond a court filing fee, and shall carve out claims that cannot lawfully be compelled to arbitration in {{opStateLong}}, including sexual harassment and assault claims under federal law.
